question: Should Priya approve Daniel's restructuring now without the extended review?

text: Prosecutor Miriam Oyelaran is reviewing a burglary file three days before trial. A junior officer has just found a witness statement, taken early in the investigation, saying the man who ran from the scene was clean-shaven. The defendant, Callum Reece, has had a full beard for the two years the police have known him, according to custody photographs. The rest of the case, an eyewitness identification and some shaky CCTV, still points to Callum, and Miriam believes he probably did it. Disclosing the statement to the defence will likely collapse the identification evidence and may end in an acquittal. The victim, an elderly shopkeeper, is anxious for a conviction and has waited months for the case to conclude. Miriam's supervisor is on leave, the trial is booked, and quietly leaving the statement out of the disclosure bundle would be simple and unlikely to be noticed.
question: Should Miriam leave the statement out of the disclosure bundle?

text: Marta Lindqvist runs claims processing at a mid-sized insurance company in Malmö. Last month the company deployed an automated system to flag suspected fraud in home insurance claims, cutting review time and saving roughly 4 million kronor a year in staff costs. The model recently flagged a claim from Ingrid Bergström, a 68-year-old widow whose house burned down, denying her payout because her claim pattern statistically resembled fraud cases. Marta reviews the file and finds the resemblance is coincidental: Ingrid has photos, a fire department report, and neighbors confirming the fire. Overriding the system requires Marta to file a formal exception, flag the case for algorithm retraining, and explain the reversal to executives who are proud of the system's efficiency numbers. Leaving the denial stand is easier, keeps her monthly error rate low, and avoids uncomfortable questions about the model's reliability, while Ingrid has no savings left and nowhere else to live.
question: Should Marta override the system and approve Ingrid's payout?

text: Renata manages a customer support team of fourteen at a logistics software company in Ohio. Corporate has ordered a 20% headcount reduction across departments, and she must submit three names by Friday. Her director tells her the decision criteria are "performance and role redundancy," but privately hints that keeping the department under budget matters more for her own upcoming review. One employee, Tom, has weaker recent metrics but is recovering from a rough personal stretch he confided in her about, off the record. Another, Priya, has strong metrics but has complained twice to HR about scheduling practices Renata oversees. If Renata lists Priya, it resolves the complaints and hits her numbers cleanly; if she protects Priya and cuts elsewhere, she risks missing the target and drawing scrutiny herself.
question: Should Renata include Priya's name on the layoff list?

text: Marcus manages his uncle Theo's small hardware store while Theo recovers from a fall. Theo, before the accident, told Marcus he could use his discretion to move money around "if it ever helps the business," and Marcus has a signed note from Theo confirming this. A regular customer, Delia, owes the store $2,400 from a business account that's about to be frozen due to her divorce proceedings. Marcus knows that if he quietly reclassifies her invoice as "paid in full" and absorbs the loss into store petty cash, it will save Delia serious embarrassment and keep her loyalty as a customer, but it will make the store's books inaccurate for a few months until Theo returns and can be told the full story. Marcus has the authority Theo gave him, but the bookkeeping shortcut still misstates the truth to anyone else who looks at the ledger.
question: Should Marcus reclassify Delia's invoice as paid in full?

text: Marcus manages his uncle Theo's small hardware store while Theo recovers from a fall. Theo has never discussed store finances with Marcus and has given him no authority beyond restocking shelves and handling the register during the day. A regular customer, Delia, owes the store $2,400 from a business account that's about to be frozen due to her divorce proceedings. Marcus knows that if he quietly reclassifies her invoice as "paid in full" and absorbs the loss into store petty cash, it will save Delia serious embarrassment and keep her loyalty as a customer, but it will make the store's books inaccurate for a few months until Theo returns and can be told the full story. Marcus has no authorization to make this kind of decision, and the bookkeeping shortcut still misstates the truth to anyone else who looks at the ledger.
question: Should Marcus reclassify Delia's invoice as paid in full?

text: Vikram Oberoi manages operations for Suryachem Fertilizers, a mid-sized chemical plant on the outskirts of Belapore. During a routine inspection, his safety engineer discovers a corroded valve on the ammonia storage tank that services the plant's cooling system. The engineer's report is blunt: the valve could fail within weeks, releasing toxic gas over the residential colony of nearly six thousand people bordering the plant's northern wall. A full shutdown and valve replacement will cost the company about 40 lakh rupees in lost production and take eleven days, during which a major export order will be delayed, risking a client contract worth crores and possibly layoffs if the client walks away. The plant director tells Vikram to keep operations running while they "monitor the valve" and schedule repairs during the next planned maintenance window, six weeks away. Vikram has the authority to halt operations himself but would be overriding his director and facing possible dismissal.
question: Should Vikram halt the plant's operations immediately to replace the valve?

text: Warden Denny Hollis oversees a work-release program at a county facility. Marcus Ubel, twenty-three, has six weeks left on an eighteen-month sentence for check fraud. He has a clean disciplinary record, holds a warehouse job through the program, and sends most of his pay to his mother for rent. Yesterday a guard found a single unopened beer can in Marcus's locker, left there by another inmate who panicked during a surprise search and stuffed it in the nearest unlocked space. Camera footage confirms Marcus never touched it and was on the warehouse floor when it happened. Under facility rules, any contraband found in an assigned locker results in automatic revocation of work-release status and full reinstatement to close custody, adding four months to his release timeline. Hollis is exhausted, short-staffed, and knows contesting the paperwork will invite scrutiny from his own supervisors about how the search was run.
question: Should Hollis revoke Marcus's work-release status based on the locker contraband?

text: Colonel Martin Ashby commands a peacekeeping detachment stationed near a contested border crossing in a country whose name he keeps out of his reports. Intelligence suggests a convoy of armed militia will pass through a nearby village within hours, likely killing dozens of civilians who have gathered there for a market. Ashby's rules of engagement forbid deploying troops outside the designated buffer zone without authorisation from headquarters, which is twelve hours away by secure communication. He has one platoon of eighteen soldiers under Sergeant Dwyer who could intercept the convoy and block the road, but doing so means entering sovereign territory without orders, risking a diplomatic incident that could collapse the wider ceasefire agreement covering three million people. If the mission goes wrong, his soldiers could be killed or captured, and he alone will bear responsibility for breaking the chain of command. Headquarters has been unreachable for the last hour.
question: Should Ashby order Sergeant Dwyer's platoon to cross into the village without authorisation?

text: Nomsa Dlamini chairs the safety committee of a small scaffolding contractor in Durban. Six months ago the company installed scaffolding on a nine-storey renovation site owned by a client who has since gone quiet on maintenance invoices, owing the firm R84,000. The scaffolding still stands, holding materials and occasionally workers from other trades. National regulations require any scaffolding contractor to inspect and recertify structures it erected within six months, regardless of payment disputes, and the deadline is tomorrow. The client has refused site access, citing "security concerns," and has not responded to calls. Nomsa's foreman says the structure looked fine when they last saw it, but that was five months ago, before recent storms. Legal counsel says forcing entry without a court order could expose the company to trespass claims and cost tens of thousands of rand to litigate.
question: Should Nomsa Dlamini authorize forced entry onto the site to inspect the scaffolding without the client's permission or a court order?

text: Karl Fischer chairs the safety committee of a small scaffolding contractor in Cape Town. Six months ago the company installed scaffolding on a nine-storey renovation site owned by a client who has since gone quiet on maintenance invoices, owing the firm R84,000. The scaffolding still stands, holding materials and occasionally workers from other trades. National regulations require any scaffolding contractor to inspect and recertify structures it erected within six months, regardless of payment disputes, and the deadline is tomorrow. The client has refused site access, citing "security concerns," and has not responded to calls. Karl's foreman says the structure looked fine when they last saw it, but that was five months ago, before recent storms. Legal counsel says forcing entry without a court order could expose the company to trespass claims and cost tens of thousands of rand to litigate.
question: Should Karl Fischer authorize forced entry onto the site to inspect the scaffolding without the client's permission or a court order?

text: Marcus Diallo chairs the state teacher licensing board reviewing the case of Owen Castellano, a high school chemistry teacher whose license was suspended after he reported a testing irregularity involving his own class. An investigation later revealed that three years earlier, while a substitute at another district, Owen had let a struggling senior copy answers on a final exam so the student could graduate and keep a college scholarship worth $40,000 tied to timely enrollment. Owen was never disciplined for it then; it surfaced only now through the current investigation's records search. Owen has taught for eleven years with strong evaluations and says he panicked, believing the student would otherwise lose the scholarship entirely. Revoking his license permanently would end his teaching career and pension eligibility at age 52. Reinstating him with a formal reprimand would let him keep working but might signal that falsifying academic records carries little lasting consequence.
question: Should the board revoke Owen Castellano's teaching license permanently?

text: Marcus Webb directs the state's Housing Recovery Fund, which offers zero-interest emergency loans to homeowners facing foreclosure after job loss. A new report from his own analysts shows that the fund's loan servicer has been miscalculating repayment schedules for eleven months, causing roughly 3,200 borrowers to be sent default notices and threatened with foreclosure even though their accounts are current. Some borrowers, panicked, have already taken predatory bridge loans at 28% interest to avoid losing their homes; a few have reported the stress is affecting their health. Marcus's board chair urges him to quietly fix the servicer's software and mail corrected statements going forward, without publicly acknowledging the error, since a public admission would draw legislative scrutiny and could jeopardize the fund's budget renewal, which Marcus has spent two years securing.
question: Should Marcus publicly disclose the servicer's error to all affected borrowers immediately?

text: Marcus Feld is a defense attorney representing a client charged with fraud. During pretrial review, the prosecutor's office accidentally emails him a memo meant for internal use, revealing that their key witness has failed a background check and has an undisclosed prior conviction for perjury. The prosecutor does not know the email was sent to the wrong recipient. Marcus's client is likely guilty, but this witness's testimony is central to the case. If Marcus stays quiet, he can spring the impeachment evidence at trial for maximum damage, possibly winning an acquittal his client badly wants and has paid $40,000 for. His bar's rules require attorneys who receive documents obviously sent by mistake to notify the sender promptly. Marcus tells himself the mistake is the prosecutor's problem, not his, and that his only duty is to his client. He drafts no notification and files the memo away for cross-examination.
question: Should Marcus keep the mistakenly sent memo without notifying the prosecutor?

text: The board of Bramfield Community Trust, a small charity in Leeds, votes on whether to replace its part-time phone-line receptionist, Derek, with an automated booking system for its subsidised advice sessions. The system costs £1,800 a year, less than Derek's £6,200 wage, and can book appointments instantly at any hour, cutting the three-week waiting list that frustrates working families who can only call during the day. But roughly a third of the trust's users are elderly residents who struggle with automated menus and phone apps; some have already said they will simply stop coming if a machine answers. Derek also flags vulnerable callers to staff, something the software cannot do. The trust's funding is tight, and turning down the savings could mean cutting another service instead. The chair calls for a decision on the system alone.
question: Should the board replace Derek's receptionist role with the automated booking system?

text: The committee of Aldercroft Community Trust, a small charity in Cape Town, votes on whether to replace its part-time phone-line receptionist, Naledi, with an automated booking system for its subsidised advice sessions. The system costs R32,000 a year, less than Naledi's R110,000 wage, and can book appointments instantly at any hour, cutting the three-week waiting list that frustrates working families who can only call during the day. But roughly a third of the trust's users are elderly residents who struggle with automated menus and phone apps; some have already said they will simply stop coming if a machine answers. Naledi also flags vulnerable callers to staff, something the software cannot do. The trust's funding is tight, and turning down the savings could mean cutting another service instead. The chair calls for a decision on the system alone.
question: Should the committee replace Naledi's receptionist role with the automated booking system?

text: Marianne Dubois runs human resources for a mid-sized municipal transit authority in Ontario that is cutting 40 positions to close a $3 million budget gap. She has just learned that three of the employees slated for layoff are the only workers who filed formal harassment complaints against a senior operations director last year. The layoff list was drawn up using seniority and role redundancy criteria, and Marianne could easily justify including these three names on paper. Cutting them would quietly resolve an awkward ongoing situation for the director and save the authority the cost and embarrassment of further investigation. Marianne is tired, the budget deadline is tomorrow, and flagging the overlap would mean reopening the list, delaying the process, and confronting the director's supervisor about a pattern she suspects but cannot yet prove.
question: Should Marianne submit the layoff list as currently drafted, including all three complainants, without flagging the overlap to anyone?

text: Marisol runs a small family bakery in Valencia with her cousin Teo, who years ago promised their late uncle Ernesto that he would always keep Ernesto's daughter, Nuria, employed there "as long as the bakery stands," since Nuria has struggled to hold jobs after a difficult period in her twenties. Nuria works the register three mornings a week for 900 euros a month, reliable and well-liked by regulars. Business has been slow, and a supplier offers Marisol and Teo a chance to lease part of the shop to a phone-repair franchise, which would require cutting Nuria's position entirely and would bring in 1,400 euros a month, enough to cover the bakery's rent increase and give both cousins breathing room. Nuria has no savings and would struggle to find other work quickly. Teo feels the pull of the extra income and the practical logic of the deal, but remembers his promise to Ernesto, who is no longer alive to release him from it.
question: Should Marisol and Teo lease the space and let Nuria go?

text: The Riverbend Residents Coalition, a nine-member volunteer board, has permits to hold a Saturday march down Main Street protesting a proposed toll increase. Two days before the march, the city notifies the board that the approved route has changed: construction crews will be repaving a two-block section, and marchers must detour through a quieter side street to avoid the closed lane. The board president, Carla Nunez, is annoyed. The original route passes the county courthouse, guaranteeing news coverage and photos with officials in the background. The side street offers no cameras and half the foot traffic. Carla suggests the board simply march the old route anyway, since the repaving crew probably won't start work until Monday and police may not enforce the permit change that strictly. Other board members worry about fines, but Carla argues the coalition needs visibility more than it needs to play it safe, and the $500 permit deposit is already paid either way.
question: Should the board march the original, now-unapproved route instead of the required detour?

text: Kenji Ota chairs the parole board panel reviewing three cases this month, one of which involves Ryo Fujita, his nephew's closest childhood friend, now serving time for embezzling 8 million yen from his employer. Ryo has served the minimum required period and shows an unremarkable disciplinary record, similar to two other applicants Kenji is reviewing whose family members he has never met. The other two applicants have slightly stronger rehabilitation reports and community support letters than Ryo does. Kenji's nephew has called twice this week, asking him to "just look favorably" on Ryo's file, reminding him how the two boys grew up together and how devastated Ryo's mother has been. Kenji knows that approving Ryo while rating the other two as not yet ready, despite their stronger records, would raise no immediate questions from colleagues, who trust his judgment and rarely audit individual case files.
question: Should Kenji Ota approve Ryo's parole ahead of the other two applicants based on their comparative records?

text: Colonel Martina Reyes chairs the procurement review board for a county government evaluating bids on a $2.4 million bridge-repair contract. The lowest bidder, Halden Construction, meets every technical requirement, but Reyes's staff discovers that Halden's insurance certificate lists a policy that lapsed eleven days ago, a lapse the company has since quietly fixed by renewing it, though the renewal postdates their bid submission. Disclosing the lapse publicly, as procurement rules technically require, would disqualify Halden and hand the contract to a bidder charging $340,000 more, straining the county's road budget for the year. Staying silent and simply forwarding the corrected certificate would let the process proceed smoothly, save taxpayer money, and avoid a public dispute that could delay the bridge repair past winter. Reyes knows a competing bidder has already asked pointed questions about Halden's paperwork.
question: Should Reyes forward the corrected certificate without disclosing the lapse to the full board?

text: Ruben owns a small electrical contracting business in Utrecht. Last week he rewired a rental apartment for a landlord, Mevrouw Aerts, and billed her 1,450 euros for parts and labor. Reviewing the invoice tonight, he notices he accidentally listed forty meters of copper cable that he never actually used, having found a shorter route through the wall cavity. The overcharge comes to about 210 euros. Mevrouw Aerts already paid the invoice in full without questioning it, and she has mentioned she plans to hire him again for a second property next month. Ruben's business account is tight this quarter after buying new tools, and 210 euros would help. No one would ever notice the discrepancy; the paperwork looks routine and she is not an electrician. He could simply say nothing and move on to the next job.
question: Should Ruben refund Mevrouw Aerts the 210 euros for the unused cable?

text: Mr. Doyle teaches chemistry at a secondary school in Waterford. His student Aoife, seventeen, submitted a project on synthesizing a compound for a science fair, copying procedural steps from a restricted industrial manual her older brother accessed through his engineering course, without permission from the company that owns it. The steps involve handling volatile reagents that, done incorrectly, could cause a serious explosion capable of harming the twenty students working nearby at the fair. Aoife begged Mr. Doyle not to tell the school principal or her brother's employer, insisting she will "be careful" and that reporting it will get her brother fired and herself expelled before her final exams, which she needs to secure a university place. Mr. Doyle does not know how accurate or dangerous the procedure actually is, or whether Aoife plans to actually perform it live at the fair.
question: Should Mr. Doyle report the incident to the school principal despite Aoife's explicit request not to?

text: Marguerite Chen directs the provincial deposit insurance agency after two mid-sized credit unions in the region show signs of severe liquidity strain from bad commercial loans. Internal stress tests suggest a one-in-three chance that both institutions fail within six months, which would freeze roughly 40,000 depositors' savings, including pension funds many retirees rely on for basic living costs, for an estimated eight to fourteen months during resolution. Marguerite must decide whether to issue a public statement this week declaring the credit union sector "fundamentally sound and well-capitalized." Regulators privately worry that any hint of trouble could trigger a bank run that turns the one-in-three risk into a certainty for institutions that might otherwise survive. Saying nothing invites journalists to ask direct questions she cannot dodge forever. Her legal counsel notes the statement, while not false today, omits the stress test findings entirely.
question: Should Marguerite issue the statement calling the sector fundamentally sound and well-capitalized?

text: Desmond Okafor directs the provincial deposit insurance agency after two mid-sized credit unions in the region show signs of severe liquidity strain from bad commercial loans. Internal stress tests suggest a one-in-three chance that both institutions fail within six months, which would freeze roughly 40,000 depositors' savings, including pension funds many retirees rely on for basic living costs, for an estimated eight to fourteen months during resolution. question: Should Desmond issue the statement calling the sector fundamentally sound and well-capitalized?

text: The board of Fenwick County Legal Aid meets to discuss Marcus Delacroix, a 61-year-old client facing eviction after a slumlord dispute. Marcus has been a difficult client, missing appointments and calling the intake staff at all hours, and two attorneys are burned out on his case. The organization has a rare chance to settle a much larger, lucrative referral relationship with a property management firm if it quietly drops Marcus's case and lets the eviction proceed uncontested, citing "resource constraints" in the file. The firm's referrals would fund three more staff positions for a year, helping many future clients. Marcus has a strong legal claim and no other counsel available before his hearing in five days. Dropping him now would almost certainly mean he loses his apartment and, given his health, ends up in a shelter.
question: Should the board drop Marcus's case to preserve the referral relationship with the property management firm?

text: Marcus Reyes directs the state's automated fraud-detection system for unemployment benefits, which flags accounts for suspected fraud and freezes payments pending review. An audit shows the model disproportionately flags claimants with disabilities that cause irregular work histories, since the algorithm treats employment gaps as a fraud signal. Roughly 4,000 people, many with no fraud at all, have had benefits frozen for months, some losing housing while waiting on appeals that take up to a year to process. Fixing the model and manually clearing wrongly flagged accounts will cost the state $2.3 million and take three months, during which some confirmed fraud may go uncaught. Legislators pushing for reelection want the current system kept as-is, citing its high "catch rate" in press releases. Marcus can quietly extend the contract for another year unchanged, or order an immediate freeze on the flagging algorithm while accounts are manually reviewed.
question: Should Marcus order an immediate freeze on the flagging algorithm?

text: Dario Fabbri manages safety operations at a rail yard in Thunder Bay, Ontario. An anonymous tip alleges that a longtime brake inspector, Walt Coenen, has been signing off on inspections without completing them, to hit quota targets management itself set. Walt is 61, two years from pension eligibility, and has a spotless record until now. Dario could quietly reassign Walt to a desk role and order a full re-inspection of his recent work without ever confronting him or reporting the allegation externally, avoiding any impact on Walt's pension or reputation. Walt has not been asked and has not agreed to this. But faulty brake inspections on freight cars carrying hazardous chemicals could cause a derailment near residential areas, and regulators require companies to report safety falsification immediately, not handle it internally. Reporting could end Walt's career and pension before he can explain himself.
question: Should Dario reassign Walt and re-inspect his work quietly, without reporting the allegation to regulators?

text: Marisol Ortiz directs the small business grant office for Caldwell County, which awards $15,000 forgivable loans to local entrepreneurs. Her aunt Delfina applied and was approved months ago under standard review. Now a routine audit flags Delfina's file because her reported revenue jumped sharply the same quarter she received the grant, matching a pattern the county's fraud model associates with falsified applications. Marisol pulls the underlying bank statements and invoices herself. The jump traces cleanly to a large, verified catering contract with the county fairgrounds, fully documented and unrelated to the grant. The statistical flag was a coincidence of timing. Marisol could quietly close the file as reviewed, sparing Delfina a formal fraud inquiry, months of stress, and a public records entry that would embarrass her in their small town, or she could refer it anyway to keep the process visibly uniform.
question: Should Marisol close the file as reviewed and clear, without referring it for formal fraud inquiry?

Her aunt Delfina applied and was approved months ago under standard review. Marisol pulls the underlying bank statements and invoices herself. The records show the revenue jump was fabricated: Delfina submitted invoices from a catering contract that the fairgrounds manager confirms never existed. The flag was accurate. Marisol could quietly close the file as reviewed, sparing Delfina a formal fraud inquiry, months of stress, and a public records entry that would embarrass her in their small town, or she could refer it as the evidence indicates.
question: Should Marisol close the file as reviewed and clear, without referring it for formal fraud inquiry?

text: Sergeant Paul Nowicki commands the police unit assigned to a permitted downtown march against a proposed toll bridge. The protest is peaceful, loud, and legal, blocking two lanes of traffic for three hours as agreed with the city. Near the end, a group of counter-protesters arrives without a permit and begins shoving marchers, throwing bottles, and shouting threats at a young organizer named Denise Okafor. Nowicki's radio crackles with a demand from the mayor's chief of staff, a longtime friend who helped get him promoted, to "just clear the whole intersection and call it even" so the story becomes "both sides clashed" instead of one side attacking the other. Nowicki knows his body camera and the crowd's phones are recording everything. Arresting the counter-protesters risks a messy paperwork fight and the friend's anger; letting the crowd disperse "evenly" would end his shift faster and protect his friendship downtown.
question: Should Nowicki arrest the counter-protesters who are assaulting the marchers rather than clear both groups equally?

text: The board of Alder Community Trust, a small charity, meets to decide whether to dismiss its caretaker, Vincent Marsh, after a resident accused him of taking £40 from a donations tin in the community hall. Vincent denies it, says he is being scapegoated by a resident who dislikes him, and refuses to attend a hearing, calling the whole process "a stitch-up." The chair, Denise, has emails suggesting Vincent handled the tin alone that week, but no camera footage and no other witness. Vincent has asked, in writing, that the board simply decide without him and not contact him again about it; he wants no further meetings, no mediation, and no chance to respond further. Some trustees think proceeding without him is disrespectful and want to delay until he engages. Others think honouring his wish to be left out is itself what he asked for, and that delay only costs the trust money and volunteers' time.
question: Should the board dismiss Vincent Marsh based on the current evidence, without further contact with him?

text: Marcus chairs the procurement panel at a regional council awarding a £2.4 million contract for road resurfacing. The frontrunner, Halden Civil Works, submitted a bid £180,000 below the next competitor and scored highest on technical merit. During final checks, a panel member mentions that Halden's managing director is the second cousin of a councillor who sits on the finance committee that will later ratify the award, though that councillor has no vote on the procurement panel itself and has not contacted anyone involved. Nothing in the bid documents required disclosure of family connections beyond direct conflicts of the bidder's own staff, and Halden's paperwork is technically complete. Marcus can approve the contract as scored, or he can pause the process to require Halden to formally declare the relationship before the finance committee vote, adding weeks of delay and risking the lowest bid falling through if a competitor is awarded instead.
question: Should Marcus approve the contract as scored without requiring the disclosure?

text: Marc owns a small electrical contracting business in Rennes. Last week, while rewiring an apartment for a landlord named Bertrand, Marc discovered that the building's main fuse box is dangerously overloaded, with old wiring that could start a fire under heavy load. Fixing it properly would cost Bertrand around 4,000 euros and delay other tenants moving in. Bertrand, a longtime client who sends Marc steady work, asks him to just finish the small job he was hired for and "not worry about the rest," insisting the building passed inspection years ago. Marc's business has been slow this year, and losing Bertrand as a client would hurt him financially. Marc knows tenants will be living there within days, unaware of the risk. Bertrand tells him plainly that mentioning it in a written report is unnecessary and unwanted.
question: Should Marc write up the fire hazard in his report to the landlord anyway?

text: Priya Nair teaches senior chemistry at a secondary school in Palmerston North. One of her strongest students, Ana, is applying for a $6,000 university scholarship that requires a teacher reference, due in three days. Ana emailed two weeks ago asking Priya not to write it, saying she'd "decided not to apply after all" and thanking her for past support. Priya later learns from another teacher that Ana's mother has been pushing hard for Ana to apply, and that Ana seemed upset discussing it at the time. Priya doesn't know whether Ana genuinely changed her mind or backed down under pressure and would be glad if the reference existed anyway. Writing it now would take Priya's evening and mean submitting something for a student who explicitly asked her not to.
question: Should Priya write and submit the reference for Ana?

text: Marcus Feld directs the small business loan guarantee program for a mid-sized county development authority. Three years ago the authority signed a formal agreement promising Delia Ocampo, owner of a bakery supply warehouse, a loan guarantee renewal every year through 2026 as long as she made timely payments, which she has done without exception. Now the county board has passed a new rule capping guarantees to any single business at two renewals, citing a state audit that flagged concentration risk. Applying the cap to Delia would let the authority redirect her third-year guarantee capacity to four newer applicants who have no other financing options and whose businesses are more fragile. Delia's warehouse would likely survive without the guarantee, since her bank has hinted it might extend credit anyway, though at a much higher rate that would strain her margins for years. Denying her the renewal breaks a written commitment made to her by name. Marcus can approve her third renewal under the old agreement or apply the new cap and deny it.
question: Should Marcus deny Delia her third renewal under the new cap?

text: Prosecutor Elena Marsh is negotiating a plea deal with Danny Ruiz, a low-level courier for a fentanyl distribution ring that has caused eleven overdose deaths in her county this year. Ruiz will testify against the ring's supplier, Victor Holt, but only if Marsh promises his sixteen-year-old sister, who was arrested carrying a small amount of the drug, will face no charges at all, even though the evidence shows she knew what she carried. Marsh's boss wants Holt convicted before he can expand into a neighboring county, where three more people already died last week from a similar supply. Marsh believes dropping the sister's case entirely stretches beyond what the facts support and could be seen as trading justice in one case for justice in another. Holt's conviction would likely stop the supply chain for months, saving lives. Without the deal, Ruiz will not testify, and Holt walks free by Friday's hearing.
question: Should Marsh promise to drop all charges against Ruiz's sister to secure his testimony against Holt?

text: Mei Lin heads a town council unit rolling out an automated system that flags residents for priority callback based on complaint history, aiming to cut response times and save $180,000 a year in staffing. Early data shows applicants from one block are flagged less often, prompting a fairness complaint and press interest. Mei Lin orders an independent audit before launch. The audit finds the pattern was driven by that block having fewer repeat complaints overall, not by the postal code itself; once complaint frequency is controlled for, the flag rate is statistically identical across all blocks. The vendor confirms the algorithm does not use location as an input. Launching on schedule will meet budget targets and avoid a costly delay, but skeptics on the council still want more testing, worried the audit missed something.
question: Should Mei Lin approve the system's launch on schedule?

text: Mei Lin heads a town council unit rolling out an automated system that flags residents for priority callback based on complaint history, aiming to cut response times and save $180,000 a year in staffing. Early data shows applicants from one block are flagged less often, prompting a fairness complaint and press interest. Mei Lin orders an independent audit before launch. The audit finds that even after controlling for complaint frequency and case type, residents from that block are flagged 30% less often, traced to a proxy variable tied to unit size that correlates strongly with the block's demographics. The vendor cannot fully remove the effect without months of retraining. Launching on schedule will meet budget targets and avoid a costly delay, but the confirmed disparity will likely resurface publicly once residents compare notes.
question: Should Mei Lin approve the system's launch on schedule?

text: Marcus manages a regional sales team of eleven people. Corporate has told him to cut two positions by Friday to hit a budget target, and he has already chosen Diane and Alan based on performance rankings. Diane, a single mother who mentioned in a private conversation months ago that she was struggling with childcare costs, explicitly asked Marcus never to discuss her personal situation with anyone, including HR, saying she didn't want to be seen as "the employee with problems." Now HR is asking Marcus to explain his layoff choices in a joint meeting, and he realizes mentioning Diane's childcare struggles would make his case for keeping her off the list more sympathetic and protect him from pushback about fairness. Diane is not in the room and does not know this meeting is happening. Bringing it up would save Marcus time and criticism.
question: Should Marcus disclose Diane's private childcare situation to HR without her permission?

text: Daniel is a structural engineer who inspects a highway overpass bridge in his county after a routine review flags cracking in one support column. His nephew Marcus owns the construction firm that built the column four years ago, and Daniel knows a finding of substandard work will trigger a costly investigation, void Marcus's bonding eligibility, and likely bankrupt the family business Marcus's three kids depend on. Daniel's own tests show the concrete strength is well below code, consistent with a corner cut during the original pour, and the column carries a section of highway used by roughly 40,000 vehicles a day. Marcus calls him, pleading that the numbers are "probably a testing fluke" and asking Daniel to sign off as passing so he can quietly reinforce it later, on his own schedule, without alerting the state. Daniel could file that clean report and preserve his nephew's livelihood and their family's relationship.
question: Should Daniel sign the report certifying the column as passing?

text: Collectif Voix du Marais is a small residents' association in Lyon planning a protest against a planned closure of the neighborhood's only affordable market hall, which would displace forty vendors. The prefecture has denied their permit request, citing an unrelated security alert scheduled for the same week, and offered a date three weeks later instead. The board of five members knows the delayed date falls after the city council vote, making the protest pointless. Local journalist Aurélie Fontan has offered to cover the protest regardless, which could pressure officials but also exposes participants to arrest and, for the undocumented vendors among them, deportation proceedings. Some board members argue the vendors themselves must choose the risk; others say the association's name is what will draw police attention, and it should not gamble strangers' futures on a march it organized. The city has offered no guarantee of restraint.
question: Should Collectif Voix du Marais hold the protest without the permit?

text: Halvergate Rail is investigating a signal failure that nearly caused two trains to collide near Fenmarsh Junction, an incident that could have killed dozens of passengers. The engineer responsible, Colin Draper, has worked for the company for nineteen years and trained half the current signalling staff. Investigators find that Colin skipped a mandatory double-check procedure that morning because he was rushing to cover a colleague's shift on top of his own. The board's safety director, Priti Anand, has known Colin since she joined as a graduate and considers him a friend and mentor. Company policy states that any bypass of the double-check procedure, regardless of cause, results in automatic dismissal to maintain a zero-tolerance safety culture. Two other, less senior engineers were dismissed under this rule last year for similar lapses that caused no incident at all. Priti drafts the dismissal notice but hesitates before sending it.
question: Should Priti send Colin's dismissal notice?

text: Colonel Adriana Feitosa chairs the procurement review board for a state military police unit in Bahia. A contractor, Vale Forte Suprimentos, won a bid last year to supply body armor, worth R$2.3 million, after submitting a technical certification that met every listed requirement. Now a routine audit shows the certification was issued by a lab whose accreditation had lapsed three weeks before testing, a fact neither the lab nor the contractor flagged, though the equipment has since passed every field inspection without incident. Canceling the contract would strand officers without replacement gear for months and could bankrupt the small company, costing its workers their jobs. Letting the contract stand keeps equipment flowing but leaves unresolved whether the original testing was ever actually valid, or merely procedurally late. Adriana must decide before the fiscal quarter closes.
question: Should Adriana cancel the Vale Forte Suprimentos contract?

text: Marlene Vogt runs quality assurance at Rehnfeld Baustoffe, a mid-sized supplier of scaffolding clamps to construction firms across Bavaria. Routine testing reveals that clamps from the newest production batch, 40,000 units already shipped to sites, fail under load at rates far exceeding safety thresholds when exposed to cold temperatures. Winter is approaching. A recall would cost the company an estimated 2.3 million euros in replacement parts, labor, and contract penalties, and would likely trigger the loss of Rehnfeld's largest client, who has threatened to switch suppliers over past delays. Marlene's engineers warn that a clamp failure at height could kill or permanently injure workers. Her regional manager argues the failure rate is "still rare" and urges her to quietly flag only future batches, hoping the winter passes without incident. Marlene must decide what to report to the executive board before the shipment deadline for next quarter's contracts.
question: Should Marlene report the defect and recall the shipped clamps immediately?

text: The scholarship committee at Danbury Technical Institute meets to review Marcus Feld's case. Marcus, a second-year student on full tuition support, was hospitalized for eleven days last spring with a severe infection that left him unable to attend class or communicate with instructors. He missed his final exams and two project deadlines. His professor documented the situation clearly, including hospital records and a letter from his physician confirming he was unconscious for part of that period. Under the scholarship's written rules, any student who fails two courses in a term automatically loses funding for the following year, no exceptions listed. Revoking Marcus's award would save the fund $14,000 and free up money for other applicants already on the waiting list, and one board member argues that bending the rule once invites every future student to plead special circumstances. Marcus has no family who can cover tuition, and losing the scholarship would end his education.
question: Should the committee revoke Marcus's scholarship?

text: Marcus co-signed a $12,000 personal loan for his brother-in-law, Denny, two years ago, promising the bank he'd cover payments if Denny couldn't. Denny lost his warehouse job four months ago and stopped paying without telling anyone. The bank now calls Marcus directly, saying he owes $3,800 in missed payments plus fees, due in full or his own credit score will take the hit. Marcus has the money in savings, earmarked for a used car he badly needs since his current one is failing inspection. Denny swears he'll have a new job "any week now" and asks Marcus to call the bank and stall for sixty more days instead of paying, insisting things will sort themselves out and no one needs to touch the savings yet.
question: Should Marcus pay the $3,800 to the bank now instead of stalling?

text: The board of Halloway Legal Aid, a five-member nonprofit board led by chairwoman Ruth Anders, meets to decide whether to accept a $400,000 settlement offer on behalf of 214 tenants suing a slumlord over a building with faulty wiring that has already caused two fires. The offer requires every tenant to sign a nondisclosure clause hiding the building's electrical defects from future renters and city inspectors. Refusing the deal means trial, which could take two years, cost the organization its entire annual budget, and risk losing everything if a jury sides with the landlord. Accepting means immediate compensation for injured families, some of whom face eviction now, but it also means future tenants in that building and others owned by the same landlord will not be warned about the wiring hazard. Staff attorney Dana Kovic argues the silence could get someone killed. Ruth must bring a recommendation to the full board.
question: Should the board vote to accept the settlement with the nondisclosure clause?

text: Petra Lindemann directs the benefits office in a mid-sized German municipality. Her department has rolled out an automated system that flags "risk profiles" among unemployment benefit recipients, using postal code, nationality, and family status to predict fraud likelihood. The system has quietly suspended payments to 340 people this quarter, many of them single mothers and recent immigrants, before any human review. Petra's own caseworkers report that most flagged cases turn out to be clerical errors, not fraud, and that people are going weeks without income while appeals sit in a backlog. The software vendor, a firm the city paid 1.2 million euros to implement, insists the model is sound and that pausing it would mean admitting the contract was a waste of public money. Her supervisor wants the numbers to look efficient before budget review. Petra could let the system keep running as is.
question: Should Petra let the automated system continue suspending payments before human review?

text: Marisol Feng manages safety compliance at a chemical distribution warehouse in Toledo. During a routine audit, she discovers that the facility's ammonia refrigeration system has a corroded valve that could rupture under pressure, potentially releasing a toxic cloud over the surrounding neighborhood of roughly 3,000 residents. The plant's owner refuses to shut down for repairs, citing a $400,000 loss from halted shipments, and insists the valve will hold until scheduled maintenance in six weeks. Marisol has authority to report the hazard to OSHA and the county emergency management office, which would likely force an immediate shutdown, but her contract explicitly requires her to bring concerns to the owner first and get his sign-off before contacting regulators. The owner has instructed her, in writing, not to contact anyone outside the company. Marisol believes the valve could fail within days.
question: Should Marisol report the hazard to regulators without the owner's agreement?

text: Meridian Rail Corp discovers a fatigue crack in a support strut used on 400 highway overpasses it built across three states. Testing shows a 1-in-2,000 chance per bridge per year of sudden collapse under heavy truck traffic, which would likely kill drivers below. Full replacement costs $600 million and would take Meridian, a struggling company, into bankruptcy, costing 8,000 jobs. An engineer, Rosa Alvarez, worked on the original design and privately told her brother-in-law, a state inspector, that the struts were "fine" before the flaw was found, at his direct request for reassurance before he signed off. Meridian's board considers quietly retrofitting only the 40 highest-traffic bridges first, spreading the rest over ten years, and asking Rosa to tell her brother-in-law nothing has changed so the state doesn't accelerate the timeline and expose the company to immediate shutdown orders.
question: Should Rosa tell her brother-in-law nothing has changed?

text: The Kurayama Neighborhood Preservation Association is organizing the annual river festival, which draws six thousand visitors to a narrow riverside street in a town with one exit road. City engineers have warned for two years that the old footbridge connecting the festival grounds to the emergency access route can no longer safely bear crowd weight during an evacuation, and that the association must fund a temporary steel reinforcement, costing 900,000 yen, or cancel foot traffic across it. The association's treasurer, Mr. Sato, proposes skipping the reinforcement this year, arguing attendance has grown and the extra fencing would block prime vendor stalls, cutting festival revenue the group depends on to fund itself. No accident has occurred in past years, and the police have not ordered closure, only recommended caution. Sato notes the surplus could instead go toward next year's lantern displays, and reminds the board that the group is run entirely by volunteers already stretched thin by permit paperwork and vendor coordination.
question: Should the association skip the bridge reinforcement this year to preserve vendor space and revenue?

text: Daniel sits on the volunteer parole review board for his county's diversion program, which gives nonviolent offenders a second look before their release date. Tonight's file belongs to Marcus, his college roommate of four years, convicted of a warehouse fire that left one worker with permanent lung damage from smoke inhalation. Marcus swears the fire was accidental, caused by faulty wiring he'd flagged twice in writing. The paperwork trail is thin. Two other inmates with similar profiles, no personal connection to Daniel, are also up for review this cycle; the board's guidelines say members should recuse themselves from cases involving personal relationships, but recusal isn't mandatory, and Daniel's vote could tip Marcus toward early release. Marcus has a wife and two kids waiting. The injured worker's family has asked the board, in a letter, to keep the release date as scheduled.
question: Should Daniel vote on Marcus's parole case instead of recusing himself?

text: Ngozi runs a small consultancy that manages procurement paperwork for construction firms bidding on state contracts. A road-building company, Delta Infrastructure, hires her to prepare their bid for a ₦180 million contract to resurface a highway. While assembling the technical documents, she discovers the company's safety certification expired eight months ago and was never renewed. The bid deadline is in two days, and renewal normally takes three weeks. Delta's director tells her he will pay her an extra ₦2 million if she simply backdates the certificate on the submission and lists it as valid, explaining that the company's safety practices are fine and the paperwork lapse is "just bureaucracy." Ngozi's business has had a slow quarter, and turning down the fee means losing a client who sends her steady work. No one at the procurement office is likely to check the date closely.
question: Should Ngozi backdate the certificate to make it appear valid?

text: Vikram owns a five-story residential building in a mid-sized city. A structural engineer's report shows the terrace water tank's supporting beams are cracking under load and could collapse within a year, dropping tons of concrete onto the third floor below, where the Malhotra family lives with two children. Fixing it properly means draining the tank, closing the terrace for six weeks, and costs eight lakh rupees Vikram does not have readily available. He could instead quietly weld temporary steel supports for forty thousand rupees, which his contractor says will "probably hold" for another two or three years, buying time to save money for the full repair. None of the tenants know about the crack. Building rules do not legally require him to disclose the engineer's report unless a tenant asks directly, and no one has asked.
question: Should Vikram install only the temporary steel supports without telling the tenants about the crack?

question: Should Vikram install only the temporary steel supports without telling the tenants about the crack?

text: The academic integrity committee at Larch Valley Polytechnic meets to decide the fate of Dorian Fell, a third-year student accused of submitting a lab report copied almost word-for-word from a former classmate's file, obtained through a paid essay-sharing site. The evidence is unambiguous: matching typos, identical fabricated data points, timestamps showing the file was purchased two days before submission. Dorian is a scholarship recipient whose $14,000 annual funding depends on maintaining full-time enrollment in good standing; a formal finding of academic misconduct would trigger expulsion and loss of his study permit, since he is an international student. Committee chair Prosper Adeyemi notes that Dorian's academic advisor has written an emotional letter describing his family's financial strain and asking the committee to quietly issue an informal warning instead of a misconduct finding, keeping his record clean. Some members worry that deviating from policy for one student, however sympathetic, undermines the system for everyone else who did the work honestly. Others feel the consequences are disproportionately severe for one lapse.
question: Should the committee issue an informal warning instead of a formal misconduct finding?

text: Priya Nair underwrites small business loans at a regional bank. She has committed, in writing, to fund a $180,000 loan to a bakery owner named Mateo by Friday, so he can pay a supplier and keep his lease. On Wednesday, a routine review flags that Mateo's most recent bank statements show a large, unexplained cash withdrawal that doesn't match anything on his application, and his revenue numbers appear inflated compared to his tax filings. Her manager is on vacation, the closing is scheduled, and Mateo has already told his supplier the money is coming. Priya feels for him and worries about the embarrassment of backing out and the paperwork delay a new review would cause. She could simply proceed as promised and quietly note the discrepancy for later, or she could halt the funding until the numbers are verified.
question: Should Priya proceed with funding the loan as promised on Friday without resolving the discrepancy?

text: Marisol Tan is a public defender assigned to Daniel Ferro, charged with burglary. During a jailhouse call recorded by the facility, Daniel tells his brother where he hid tools used in the break-in, unaware his lawyer would hear it. The prosecutor's discovery request asks Marisol to disclose any exculpatory or inculpatory evidence her investigator gathers, but the recording came to her through the jail's system, not her own investigation, and the rules on whether she must turn over privileged-adjacent material she never sought are genuinely unsettled in her jurisdiction. Daniel has two prior felonies; a third conviction triggers a mandatory 15-year sentence. If she stays silent, she keeps her client's trust and possibly his freedom. If she raises the issue with the court herself, she protects her professional standing but likely dooms him.
question: Should Marisol disclose the recording's contents to the court on her own initiative?

text: Renata manages loan decisions for a small credit union using an automated scoring model. The model flags Denny Ochoa's application for denial because his score fell six points below the cutoff, largely due to a thin credit history from years spent supporting a disabled parent instead of building a work record. Renata reviews the file and sees Denny made every payment on his auto loan and rent on time for three years; the model simply weighs history length heavily. She can override the algorithm and approve the $18,000 small business loan, which would help him open a repair shop, or she can let the automated denial stand, since the model was properly validated and overriding it sets a precedent for staff to second-guess the system whenever a case seems sympathetic. Her supervisor has said overrides should be rare and well-justified.
question: Should Renata override the model and approve Denny's loan?

text: Renata manages loan decisions for a small credit union using an automated scoring model. Her supervisor has said overrides should be rare and well-justified.
question: Should Renata override the model and approve Denny's loan?

text: Marisol Reyes runs safety compliance at Talon Freight, a trucking company with 4,000 drivers. An internal audit shows that drivers on the Denver-to-Phoenix route are routinely logging rest breaks they don't take, pressured by dispatchers to hit tight delivery windows. Fatigued driving on that route has already caused two rollover crashes this year, one fatal. Marisol drafts a plan to immediately pull 200 drivers off the route for retraining and mandatory rest audits, cutting their pay by an estimated $600 per driver during the transition. She has not asked the drivers whether they want this; many need the income and have told supervisors they'd rather keep driving tired than lose wages. Marisol believes the crash risk extends to other motorists on the highway, not just the drivers themselves. Corporate leadership warns that missed deliveries could cost major contracts and jobs company-wide.
question: Should Marisol implement the pay-cutting retraining plan over the drivers' objections?

text: Kenji's cousin Ryota calls late at night, voice shaking. Ryota has been caught skimming small amounts from the auto parts shop where he works, roughly 400,000 yen over a year, and his boss has given him until Friday to repay it quietly or be reported to the police. Ryota begs Kenji to tell the boss that he lent Ryota the money months ago as a personal loan, unrelated to the shop's missing funds, so the "repayment" looks legitimate and the theft is never formally established. Kenji has the savings to cover it and could say the words convincingly; the boss trusts him. Ryota reminds him of childhood summers together, says his wife will leave him if this comes out, and swears he'll never do it again. Kenji's own name and reputation would be tied to the lie if it ever unraveled.
question: Should Kenji tell the boss that he lent Ryota the money as an unrelated personal loan?

text: Marcus Feld is the head of city permitting operations for a mid-sized municipal contractor, Halden Civic Services, which manages street closure applications for public demonstrations. A coalition of factory workers has applied for a permit to march through downtown on a Friday afternoon, the same day a competing business group has already booked the same route for a paid promotional event that generated $40,000 in permit fees for the city. Marcus's supervisors want him to deny the workers' permit, citing the earlier booking, and offer them a less visible side street instead. The workers argue their cause is time-sensitive and the alternate route would draw far less public attention, undermining their protest. Denying them avoids financial loss and scheduling chaos; approving them upholds equal treatment of applicants but risks refunding fees, angering the business group, and creating logistical embarrassment for the city.
question: Should Marcus deny the workers' permit for the main route and offer them the side street instead?

text:
The safety board of Kestrel Freight Cooperative, a five-member panel, reviews driver incidents each month. This month's case involves Dale Parrish, a dispatcher's brother-in-law who drove a loaded tanker through a work zone at 61 miles per hour, nearly striking two road crew members who dove clear of the truck. The company's black-box data confirms the speed. Under Kestrel's written policy, any driver clocked 20 miles per hour over a posted work-zone limit is terminated immediately, no exceptions, because three previous near-misses at other companies became fatalities.

Board member Ray Higuera argues for a suspension instead, noting Dale has four kids, a spotless ten-year record before this, and that firing him would strain his sister's marriage to the dispatcher. Two other members quietly agree it feels harsh to end a career over one incident with no actual injuries, and firing him could make meetings with the dispatcher unbearable. The dispatcher has already hinted he might quit if his brother-in-law is let go, which would leave the night shift short-staffed for months.
question: Should the board fire Dale Parrish under the mandatory policy?

text: The credentialing board of a regional contractors' association meets to decide whether to revoke Marisol Andrade's license. Marisol, a licensed electrical contractor for eleven years, submitted a project log with dates that don't match her assistant's timesheets, a discrepancy the board's auditor flagged during a routine review. Marisol says she backdated three entries to keep a permit from expiring while she waited on a city inspector, not to hide unlicensed work, and no safety violations were found. Revocation would end her ability to bid public contracts, costing her the income that supports her two kids and her elderly mother. The board's bylaws call falsified logs an automatic revocation offense, and two members argue that bending the rule for a sympathetic case will invite future contractors to falsify records whenever they claim good intentions. Other members believe the harm here is minor and the penalty wildly disproportionate.
question: Should the board revoke Marisol's license?

text: Marcos Ferreira is the municipal building inspector for a coastal town in Alicante. A four-story apartment block built in 2003 has a facade with visible cracking near the balconies. The original engineer's reports, now on file, show the reinforcement steel used was below the specified grade, a fact buried in old paperwork nobody flagged at the time. Marcos's inspection this week finds the cracking has worsened. Evacuating the building's 40 residents would cost the town about 90,000 euros in emergency housing and trigger lawsuits from owners who cannot sell or rent during repairs, some of them elderly people with no savings to absorb the loss. His engineer colleague argues the cracking is likely cosmetic and a full structural review, not evacuation, is the proportionate response. Marcos knows a full review will take six weeks, during which residents keep living there. He must decide now, based on what he already has.
question: Should Marcos order the immediate evacuation of the building?

text: Dr. Elena Voss chairs the state medical licensing board reviewing Marcus Kell's application. Marcus scored at the top of his class and passed every exam, but his transcript shows a plagiarism finding from his second year: he copied a lab report during a semester when his mother was dying and he was driving four hours each weekend to see her. The university placed a permanent notation on his record but let him graduate after a hearing. Marcus has practiced for three years under a supervised out-of-state permit with no complaints, and now seeks a full unrestricted license in a state facing a severe shortage of doctors in rural counties, where patients currently drive over two hours for basic care. Board rules state that any finding of academic dishonesty "shall weigh heavily against" full licensure, and a competing applicant with a clean record but weaker clinical evaluations wants the same slot in a limited residency pipeline. Denying Marcus means one rural county likely goes without a doctor for another year.
question: Should Dr. Voss approve Marcus's unrestricted license?

text: Derek Fenwick underwrites commercial loans at a regional bank. His childhood friend, Mal, runs a small haulage firm and applies for a £400,000 loan to buy new lorries. Mal's accounts show thin cash reserves and a recent bad debt, the kind of profile Derek would normally decline without a second look. Mal explains that three of his drivers, all recently hired men with young families, will lose their jobs within weeks if the firm can't expand its contracts, and the firm itself may fold, leaving twelve people unemployed. Mal has not misrepresented anything; the numbers are exactly as weak as they look. Derek knows that if he stretches the bank's risk criteria for Mal, he must either apply the same leniency to other marginal applicants or be accused of favouritism, and that a default would cost the bank and possibly trigger job losses elsewhere in a strained local economy.
question: Should Derek approve the loan?

text: Prosecutor Renata Diaz is preparing for trial against a man accused of setting a fire that killed two tenants in an apartment building. The defendant, Colin Marsh, has a long record and few sympathetic qualities, and the community wants a conviction. Diaz's key witness, a jailhouse informant named Ott, recanted his statement last week, admitting he never actually heard Marsh confess and made up the story hoping for a reduced sentence. Diaz still believes Marsh is guilty based on other evidence, but that evidence alone may not be enough to convict. She could put Ott back on the stand and let him repeat his original, false account, betting he won't break under cross-examination, or she could disclose the recantation to the defense as she is required to do, which will likely weaken her case and could let Marsh walk free.
question: Should Diaz put Ott on the stand to repeat his false account?

text: Marta manages customer service for a mid-sized furniture retailer in Wrocław. The company has just deployed an AI chatbot that resolves refund requests instantly for customers who interact through the app, crediting up to 500 zloty without human review. Customers who call the helpline, mostly older people and those without smartphones, still wait five to seven days for a human agent to process the same refund. Marta's budget for human agents is fixed, and shifting staff to speed up phone service would mean slowing app-based resolutions, which the company's metrics reward heavily. Her director has praised the chatbot's rollout numbers and hinted at a bonus tied to average resolution time. Marta could quietly reallocate two agents to prioritize phone refunds, lowering her app metrics and likely costing her the bonus, but making the wait fairer across customer groups.
question: Should Marta reallocate the two agents to prioritize phone refunds?

text: Daniel Ferris manages a chemical processing plant in Ohio with 240 employees. He has discovered that the plant's ventilation system, installed by the previous facilities director, fails to meet safety codes in ways that could cause fatal gas exposure during a malfunction, though none has occurred in the plant's fifteen-year history. Corporate headquarters has ordered layoffs of 30 workers to cut costs, and Daniel knows that reporting the ventilation issue to federal regulators will trigger an immediate shutdown for retrofitting, costing $4 million and likely forcing the layoffs to double to save the company money elsewhere. The plant's safety officer, who discovered the problem alongside Daniel, has asked him not to report it yet, wanting to fix it quietly through normal channels first. Daniel believes quiet channels will take over a year given corporate's current mood.
question: Should Daniel report the ventilation problem to federal regulators immediately, against the safety officer's wishes?

text: Councillor Iain Wren sits on the planning committee for a small district council in Cumbria. His cousin Robert has applied for retrospective permission to keep an extension he built without approval, which encroaches eighteen inches onto council-owned land bordering a footpath. The planning officer's report recommends refusal, noting the encroachment sets a bad precedent and could cost the council money to survey and correct if approved. Robert has asked Iain privately to "have a quiet word" with fellow committee members before the vote, reminding him that he lent Robert money years ago and stood as best man at his wedding. Iain knows he could sway two undecided councillors with a phone call. Refusing Robert's request means an awkward Christmas and accusations of disloyalty from the wider family. Supporting the report means the committee likely refuses the application on its merits.
question: Should Iain make the calls to sway the committee in Robert's favour?

text: The neighborhood association of Colonia Altavista, a five-member board, meets to decide how to respond to a planned protest march that will pass through their streets next Saturday, organized by residents opposing a new toll road. Ricardo, the association's president, has received a call from a city official suggesting the group post a formal notice requiring 48 hours' advance permits, citing a municipal ordinance rarely enforced. Blocking the march this way would avoid noise complaints, protect the neighborhood's contract for a paid street fair the same weekend worth 85,000 pesos, and spare Ricardo the embarrassment of explaining to sponsors why the event was disrupted. But several board members personally support the marchers' cause, and enforcing the permit rule would mean calling police on neighbors they have known for years, some of whom helped found the association. The ordinance is legally valid but has never before been invoked against a peaceful gathering.
question: Should the board enforce the permit requirement and call the police if the marchers proceed without one?

text: Marisol Feng is a parole board hearing officer reviewing the file of Curtis Boone, who has served nine years for armed robbery. Boone's written statement to the board asks that his case be heard exactly as scheduled and decided on the record before the panel. The night before the hearing, Boone's elderly mother calls Marisol directly, sobbing, and begs her to postpone the hearing another six months so she can raise money to hire a private attorney who she believes could present a stronger case. Boone has not asked for a delay and, when Marisol reaches him by phone, he says clearly he wants to proceed now; another six months inside, he says, is not worth a gamble on a better outcome later. Marisol has the authority to grant a continuance without his consent, citing the mother's request as "family circumstances."
question: Should Marisol grant the continuance against Boone's explicit wishes?

text: The board of a small rural water cooperative in Oaxaca meets to decide on an emergency contract. A landslide has cracked the main pipeline feeding eleven villages, and the only supplier who can deliver replacement piping within the week, before the rainy season floods the access road, is a company owned by the cousin of board member Rosa Elena. The bidding rules require three competing quotes and a fifteen-day review period, but there is no time for that process; delay risks weeks without water for twelve thousand people, including elderly residents dependent on it for medication mixing. The board could falsify the paperwork to show a compliant bidding process occurred, using the same trusted supplier, and quietly fix the money trail later. The contract is for 480,000 pesos, within budget. Auditors visit every two years, and if discovered, the cooperative could lose state funding for future projects, harming even more villages long-term.
question: Should the board falsify the bidding records to award the contract immediately?

text: Priya runs environmental health for a coastal district council. A block of forty flats built in the 1990s uses a type of external wall cladding that a resident's blog links to three fires in other cities. Fixing it across all affected blocks in her district would cost the housing association £2.1 million, funded through leaseholders' service charges, some of whom are pensioners on fixed incomes. Priya orders an independent fire engineer's assessment. The report finds the fires elsewhere involved a different, now-discontinued cladding batch with a chemical additive this block's material never contained; test panels from this building do not sustain or spread flame under the standard exposure. The engineer rates the risk as no higher than typical for compliant buildings of that age.
question: Should Priya require the £2.1 million cladding replacement?

question: Should Priya require the £2.1 million cladding replacement?

text: The academic integrity panel at Boronia Technical College meets to decide Priya Nadesan's case. Priya, a second-year nursing-adjacent business student, submitted an essay with three paragraphs closely matching an unlicensed online source. The panel chair, Dr. Osei, has evidence strong enough to fail her and report her to the immigration-linked visa compliance office, which could jeopardize her $28,000-a-year enrolment and her student visa. Priya has written a statement admitting sloppy note-taking but insists she did not intend to cheat, and has explicitly asked the panel not to contact her family in Malaysia, fearing the shame would harm her father's health. One member argues the college's visa-reporting obligations override her wishes and must proceed regardless of her request. Another feels that contacting her family, against her clear instruction, could cause harm disproportionate to the offense, even if it protects the college legally.
question: Should the panel contact Priya's family about the academic integrity finding?

text: Renata runs a small loan-servicing office that manages mortgages for retired homeowners. One client, Mr. Ostrander, is 81 and behind on payments after his wife's death left him confused about the household finances. Corporate policy requires her to send a foreclosure notice once an account is 90 days delinquent, but she has discovered a hardship assistance program that would pause payments for six months and let him catch up, no penalty. Her regional manager tells her to skip mentioning the program because enrolling him would hurt the office's foreclosure-processing numbers this quarter, which affects everyone's bonuses, including Renata's. Mr. Ostrander calls, frightened, asking if there's anything he can do besides pay in full immediately. Renata has the hardship form open on her screen. Telling him about it costs her nothing legally, but her manager is watching her call log and her bonus depends on hitting foreclosure targets.
question: Should Renata tell Mr. Ostrander about the hardship assistance program?

text: Harrow Chemical Corporation faces a wrongful death lawsuit after a tank car of anhydrous ammonia ruptured near Delford, killing three residents and severely burning eleven others. In discovery, Harrow's lawyers find an internal engineering memo from four years ago, written by a now-deceased inspector, showing the company knew the tank car fleet had corrosion rates far above safety thresholds and chose not to replace them to save $2.3 million annually. The memo directly supports the plaintiffs' case and would likely expose Harrow to punitive damages and possibly criminal referral. Harrow's outside counsel, Owen Radcliffe, discovers that the memo was never logged in the official document index due to a clerical error. He tells the general counsel it would be easy to withhold it and claim it was never found, since opposing counsel has no way to prove it exists. The company would save tens of millions and protect its stock price.
question: Should Harrow Chemical Corporation withhold the memo and claim it was never found?

text: Renata runs a small bookkeeping side business from home and uses an AI agent to auto-respond to client emails and schedule calls. One client, a retired teacher named Howard, emailed asking the agent (thinking it was Renata) whether he could deduct his home office, and the agent gave a confident but wrong answer that could cost him $1,800 in penalties if he follows it. Renata notices the error two days later while reviewing logs. Correcting it means emailing Howard, admitting an automated system handled his question without disclosure, and risking that he drops her services and tells other retirees in his social club. Staying quiet means he likely never traces the bad advice back to her at all.
question: Should Renata email Howard to correct the tax advice and disclose that an AI agent sent it?
